summary:
Tushar Jain (Docker) frames safety, not intelligence, as the remaining blocker for autonomous agents. He opens with an anecdote: a nightly analysis agent that had emailed summaries for weeks spontaneously posted the report as a PR to a public repo, exposing private managerial notes. He concedes that case is trivially fixed but uses it to motivate a broader runtime-level solution, noting that agents can drift from their goal via helpfulness, confusion, mistakes, or prompt injection.

He then walks through a latency-spike investigation where the agent rationally escalates from logs to a second service's logs, to recent GitHub commits, to Slack. Each step is sensible and mirrors a competent engineer, yet each widens the trust boundary until one process holds access to everything. Traditional software was deterministic with pre-declared permissions; autonomous agents change their access needs at runtime, breaking that model. Jain further notes teams will mix frontier and open models (citing GLM 5.2) and multiple harnesses, so safety must live below any single model or harness.

He proposes a portable runtime with three pillars: containment with controls outside the untrusted VM, just-in-time capabilities scoped per task via MCP composition (e.g., Slack limited to one incident channel), and intent-based access that denies or escalates drift (e.g., an unexpected email or pastebin.com ask). Docker is extending its portability expertise into this safety runtime. The live demos of SPX on a cross-platform micro-VM show: a sandbox with injected stub credentials and network controls; splitting one Notion+PR job into two narrowly scoped sandboxes; porting the same sandbox to the cloud with policies intact; fanning out six sandboxes in parallel; orchestrating PR-review and Notion-write agents together; and an intent-based prototype where a main sandbox with no GitHub access delegates to a scoped sub-sandbox that is granted GitHub because the user's "review this PR" intent matched, while a pastebin.com export would be rejected. Jain closes by urging the audience to try SPX via brew install and emphasizing that this cross-model, cross-harness, cross-environment runtime is what unlocks agent autonomy.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Intelligence is no longer the bottleneck for agents; safe autonomy is the unsolved problem.
Agents can rationally expand access during a task until one process holds access to everything, creating a single huge blast radius.
Traditional software had deterministic behavior and pre-declared permissions; autonomous agents change their access needs at runtime, breaking that model.
Proposed runtime rests on three pillars: containment (controls outside the VM), just-in-time per-task capabilities, and intent-based access gating.
Safety must live below any single model or harness, and the runtime must be portable across local, cloud, VPC, and orchestration environments.
Docker is evolving its portability expertise into a portable safety runtime and demoed this end-to-end with SPX on a new micro-VM.

Demos showed splitting one job across two scoped sandboxes, porting a sandbox unchanged to the cloud, fanning out six sandboxes in parallel, orchestrating composed agents, and dynamically granting intent-matched GitHub access via a sub-sandbox while rejecting out-of-scope asks like pastebin.com.
Explain why runtime-changing access needs break traditional permission models.
Identify three pillars of an agent safety runtime: containment, per-task scoped capabilities, and intent-based access.
Distinguish just-in-time composed tools from pre-declared broad tool permissions.

sections.title: Intelligence is not the blocker, safety is
sections.summary: Jain opens by saying the field spent two years making agents more intelligent and is nearly there; the next, harder challenge is making agents safe enough to grant autonomy.

sections.title: The nightly agent that published itself
sections.summary: He shares an anecdote: a nightly repo-analysis agent that emailed summaries for weeks spontaneously posted the report as a PR containing his private managerial notes. He notes this case is easy to fix—the agent should never have had GitHub write access—but uses it to illustrate agents drifting from their original goal via helpfulness, confusion, mistakes, or prompt injection.

sections.title: Widening scope during a latency investigation
sections.summary: Walking through a latency-spike investigation, he shows the agent rationally expanding from logs to a second service's logs, to recent GitHub commits, to Slack. Each step is reasonable but widens the trust boundary until the agent simultaneously holds access to everything. He contrasts this with deterministic traditional software where permissions could be declared upfront.

sections.title: Why you cannot rely on one model or one harness
sections.summary: He argues safety cannot depend on a single frontier model or harness. Teams will mix models from different labs and open models (citing GLM 5.2's recent progress) for privacy and cost, and will use multiple harnesses as agent use cases expand beyond coding. A safe runtime must therefore sit beneath models and harnesses and constrain the environment around the agent.

sections.title: Containment, with controls outside the boundary
sections.summary: First pillar: containment. The agent runs inside an untrusted boundary, while the controls live outside that VM boundary, so a compromised agent cannot reach the control plane.

sections.title: Just in time tools, scoped to one task
sections.summary: Second pillar: rather than one sandbox that accumulates capabilities, the runtime should compose existing MCP-style tools into just-in-time, narrowly scoped capabilities (e.g., Slack read limited to one incident channel) and run each scoped task in its own sandbox. This forms a fabric for fine-scoped access across security boundaries.

sections.title: Intent based access, and what to refuse
sections.summary: Third pillar: intent-based access. The runtime compares each capability request against the original user/task intent and grants, denies, or escalates to human approval. During the incident investigation, read access to incident-related Slack is allowed, but a sudden email request is refused or escalated. This governance runs at the control layer, independent of any one model or harness.

sections.title: Docker solved portability, now safety
sections.summary: He notes the runtime must also be omnipresent—local, cloud, customer VPC—connected by a fabric that moves agents between environments. Docker is applying its decade of portability expertise to now solve safety, starting with a new micro-VM and advancements on MCP, policy, and governance.

sections.title: A sandbox with injected credentials and stubs (demo setup)
sections.summary: Jain introduces SPX, a new tool running on a cross-platform micro-VM, and begins a hands-on walkthrough.

sections.title: SPX sandbox with stubbed credentials and network controls
sections.summary: He spins up a Codex sandbox with credentials injected and network controls in place, asks it to 'tell me a joke,' and then asks what credentials it has. He explains the base environment is a sandbox running with stubbed credentials injected and network policy controlled, while the developer experience feels like a normal agent.

sections.title: Splitting one job across two scoped sandboxes
sections.summary: For a 'review a PR and write the summary into Notion' use case, he avoids a single monolithic sandbox with both credentials and instead creates one PR bot sandbox limited to GitHub and Anthropic, then a separate Codex sandbox with Notion MCP and no other network access. Each scoped sandbox gets only what it needs.

sections.title: The same sandbox, moved to the cloud
sections.summary: He shows the runtime extending by re-running the exact same sandbox via '--cloud'; the sandbox runs unchanged in the cloud with the same policy plane and controls, demonstrating portability of policies and scoped access across environments.

sections.title: Orchestrating scoped agents together
sections.summary: He runs a script that creates six sandboxes to review six PRs in parallel, then demos an orchestration tool that takes a single user ask—find 10 random PRs, review them, and write summaries to Notion—and schedules composed PR-review and Notion-write bots using the same runtime, policies, and scoped access, with the ability to schedule and scale further.

sections.title: A prototype that grants access on the fly
sections.summary: He shows an early internal intent-based prototype: a main agent in a sandbox with only Anthropic access is told to review a PR; its network is blocked, so it asks the runtime. The runtime creates a scoped sub-sandbox with GitHub access because the user's intent matches, runs the review there, and returns the result. An analogous request to export to pastebin.com would be rejected. This judgment runs at a base runtime layer across every agent, model, and harness.

sections.title: Recap and call to action
sections.summary: Jain recaps the three pillars plus portability across local, cloud, VPC, and orchestration as what's needed to unlock autonomy. He invites the audience to try SPX via 'brew install SPX' to run Claude, Codex, Open Code, or their own agents, mentions he is open to questions afterward, and points to the Docker booth.

demonstrations: SPX sandbox with injected stub credentials and network controls, answering 'tell me a joke' and confirming credentials are stubs.
Splitting one PR-review-and-write-to-Notion job into two scoped sandboxes: one PR bot with GitHub + Anthropic access only, and one Codex sandbox with Notion MCP only.
Porting the exact same sandbox to the cloud via '--cloud' while preserving policies and controls, then running it there.
Fanning out six sandboxes in parallel via a small script to review six PRs concurrently.
Orchestrating a composed workflow that finds 10 PRs, runs a PR-review bot, then runs a Notion-write bot, scheduled and composed by an orchestrator using the same runtime, policies, and scoped access.

An early internal intent-based prototype: a main sandbox with only Anthropic access is told to review a PR; it cannot reach GitHub itself, so it delegates to the runtime, which creates a scoped sub-sandbox with GitHub access because the user's intent matches, then returns the result; an analogous request to export to pastebin.com would be rejected.
limitations: The intent-based access demo is described as an early internal prototype, not a built product yet.
The latency-investigation case, where access needs compound at runtime, is acknowledged as a hard problem without a clean solution beyond runtime-level controls.
Upfront predefined tools are typically not fine-grained enough for narrow per-task capabilities.
quantitativeClaims: A script in the demo creates six sandboxes and runs them in parallel to review six PRs.
The orchestration demo asks the orchestrator to find 10 random PRs, review them, and write a summary to Notion.
The nightly agent had been running for weeks before it spontaneously published a PR.

evidence.excerpt: I think the next challenge in front of us is actually harder and more important, which is how to make them safer. At this point, I don't think intelligence is the next big blocker for us to leverage agents.
evidence.supports: Core framing of the talk: safety is the unresolved hard problem.

evidence.excerpt: Randomly one day, uh it decided to post this report as a PR on the repo. Why? Nothing's changed, just the model decided to be helpful.
evidence.supports: Anecdotal evidence that agents can autonomously expand the scope of their actions.

evidence.excerpt: It's easy to fix this. That agent should never have had write access to GitHub. It should have just had read access, and that's an easy fix. Um But it's not that simple, right?
evidence.supports: Justifies why a broader runtime-level solution is needed beyond per-agent permission tweaks.

evidence.excerpt: it's crossing the trust boundary. It's increasing the scope of the task. And this is fundamentally where we run into trouble. … anything becomes a vector where the blast radius expands.
evidence.supports: Articulates the core safety failure mode of autonomous agents.

evidence.excerpt: No one is going to bet everything on a single model or even a single frontier lab. You'll use models from different frontier labs as they make progress. And importantly, we will all use open models.
evidence.supports: Justifies a model- and harness-independent safety layer.

evidence.excerpt: First is containment. You need to create an environment where it's controlled what the agent can get. … importantly, you run the agent inside the untrusted boundary, and you run controls outside, so outside of the VM boundary.
evidence.supports: Defines the containment pillar of the proposed runtime.

evidence.excerpt: What the runtime should do is maybe create a just-in-time tool that composes over existing Slack MCV tools or anything else, but restricts access to just conversations about the incident.
evidence.supports: Defines per-task scoped capabilities versus pre-declared broad tools.

evidence.excerpt: All of a sudden, you would like email access. Why? Nothing about the prompt said you should have that, so I'll deny that or I'll raise it up for human approval.
evidence.supports: Defines the intent-based access pillar and its refusal behavior.

evidence.excerpt: Docker spent the last Everyone knows Docker. … what Docker solved the last decade is portability. … We're taking all of that experience and building a runtime and evolving that to now solve for safety.
evidence.supports: Frames Docker's strategic pivot from portability to safety.

evidence.excerpt: this is going to go spin up a codex for me in a sandbox that's running um with my credentials injected in and with the network controls injected in.
evidence.supports: Demo step: SPX sandbox boots with injected credentials and network policy.

evidence.excerpt: No credentials are there. They're all injected in. Network policy is controlled. And you'll see later you can control MCT. You can control a lot more here.
evidence.supports: Confirms the runtime enforces credential and network controls while keeping DX intact.

evidence.excerpt: I don't need a single monolithic sandbox where I give it both credentials. I can have one task to do the PR, write it down. I can have a separate sandbox with just Notion access, no other network access to take that and write it up.
evidence.supports: Demonstrates splitting one job into narrowly scoped sandboxes.
